title: The flask that didn't shatter
hook: A dropped flask cracked but held together, and that led to safer windscreens.
peek: In 1903, the story goes, a French chemist knocked a glass flask off a shelf. It cracked all over but kept its shape, because a film of dried plastic lined the inside. Years later that accident became laminated glass, now used in car windscreens.
lede: Édouard Bénédictus was a French chemist, and also a painter and designer. In 1903, the story goes, he knocked an empty flask off a shelf in his laboratory. The glass cracked into a web of lines but did not fall apart. The flask had once held collodion, a solution of cellulose nitrate, which had dried into a thin, clear film that held the pieces in place.

bullets.text: Bénédictus patented the idea in 1909: a sheet of plastic sandwiched between two panes of glass. He called it Triplex, and a British company of that name went on to make safety glass for cars.

The early celluloid layer turned yellow and cloudy over time. From the 1930s makers switched to polyvinyl butyral, a clear and tough plastic that is still the usual middle layer in laminated glass today.

A car's front windscreen is laminated, so a stone chip leaves a star-shaped crack while the glass stays in one piece. Many skylights, shop windows and glass floors use the same glass and plastic sandwich.
Bénédictus is also remembered in the art world for richly coloured Art Deco pattern books, such as Variations, published in the 1920s and full of designs for fabrics and wallpapers.
